sections.heading: Thanking you for the meal you have given
sections.text: Father, thank you for the ways you give grace to your people. Help me not to treat them as empty routines, but to see your kindness in them. When I come to the Lord’s Table, remind me that you are not trying to keep me at a distance. You have set a meal before me so that my weak soul can be strengthened by Christ.
theological_themes: God gives ordinary means of grace for the strengthening of faith.
The Lord’s Supper is received as a gift of divine kindness, not as a human achievement.

scripture_references.connection: The early church devoted itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. This supports receiving the Lord’s Supper as one of the ordinary God-given practices by which believers are formed and sustained.

Paul presents the Supper as something received from the Lord and handed on to the church. The meal is not a private invention, but Christ’s own appointed way for his people to remember and proclaim his death.

sections.heading: Coming as someone who needs Christ completely
sections.text: I know I do not deserve a seat at your table. I bring no worthiness of my own. But I come because Jesus is worthy for me. I rest on what he has done, and I take refuge in his righteousness. When I hear his welcome and see his mercy, I do not want to stay away. Draw me near in love, not in presumption, but in trust.
theological_themes: Believers come to God through the merit and righteousness of Christ alone.
Christ’s gracious invitation creates humble confidence rather than fear-driven distance.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Christ, though sinless, was made sin for us so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. This grounds the prayer’s confidence in Christ’s righteousness rather than personal worthiness.
This passage calls believers to draw near to God with confidence through the blood of Jesus. It matches the prayer’s movement from unworthiness to access through Christ’s finished work.

sections.heading: Asking the Spirit to help me see Christ clearly
sections.text: Holy Spirit, wake up my faith. Do not let me handle the bread and cup carelessly or mechanically. Help me see beyond the visible signs to the Savior they point to. Teach my heart to receive him truly by faith: crucified for me, given for me, and present with his people by your grace.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit enables living faith.
The Supper requires spiritual discernment rather than mere outward participation.
The bread and cup point believers to Christ and his saving death.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the cup and bread as a participation in the blood and body of Christ, while also emphasizing the unity of believers. This supports praying for more than outward ritual: a real, faith-filled communion with Christ and his people.
Paul warns against eating and drinking in an unworthy manner and calls for discerning the body. This passage supports the prayer’s request for reverent, spiritually aware participation.

sections.heading: Remembering what Jesus suffered for me
sections.text: As I look at the bread and the cup, help me remember why Jesus died. Let me hear the gospel again: he gave his life to rescue mine. He offered himself for my sin. He shed his blood so my guilt could be removed. He was pierced so I could be cleansed. He took the curse I deserved so I could go free. He carried condemnation in my place so your justice would be satisfied and mercy could reach me without denying your holiness.
theological_themes: Atonement as sacrifice, cleansing, redemption, and satisfaction of divine justice.
The cross displays both God’s holiness and mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah describes the servant bearing griefs, being pierced for transgressions, and bringing peace through his wounds. This strongly grounds the prayer’s language of Christ suffering in the place of sinners.
Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that Jesus endured the curse in order to set his people free.

Paul explains that God justifies sinners through redemption in Christ and presents Christ’s blood in a way that demonstrates God’s righteousness. This supports the prayer’s emphasis that forgiveness comes through the cross without compromising divine justice.

sections.heading: Receiving Christ openly and gladly
sections.text: So help me come to the Table with understanding and faith. Help me reach out, take the bread, receive the cup, eat and drink, and say with my actions that I gladly receive Jesus for myself. Let this not be performance or habit. Let it be worship: reverent, honest, grateful, and full of love. Be my life, my strength, my food, my joy, and my deepest delight.
theological_themes: Faith personally receives Christ and his benefits.
Participation in the Supper is a visible confession of trust in Christ.
Christ himself is the believer’s nourishment, strength, and joy.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies himself as the bread of life and calls people to come to him and believe in him. While the passage is broader than the Lord’s Supper, it supports the prayer’s language of receiving Christ as the soul’s true nourishment by faith.

Paul says that eating the bread and drinking the cup proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes. This grounds the prayer’s idea that receiving the Supper is an open testimony to personal faith in the crucified Christ.

sections.heading: Resting in what the Supper assures me of
sections.text: At your Table, remind me again of Jesus’ eternal love, his overflowing grace, his deep compassion, his suffering, his cross, and the redemption he has won. Strengthen my assurance that, because of him, I am pardoned, adopted, alive in you, and headed for glory. As this bread and cup nourish my body, let your indwelling Spirit strengthen my soul until the day I no longer hunger or thirst, and I sit with Jesus at the feast of your kingdom.
theological_themes: The Supper strengthens assurance by directing faith to Christ’s finished work.
Believers receive pardon, adoption, life, and hope of glory in Christ.
The Lord’s Supper anticipates the final feast and fullness of life with Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects the Spirit’s witness with adoption, sonship, inheritance, suffering with Christ, and future glory. This supports the prayer’s assurance of being God’s child and heir through Christ.
This verse ties redemption and forgiveness directly to Christ’s blood and the riches of God’s grace. It grounds the prayer’s confidence that pardon is received because of Christ’s completed work.
Revelation pictures the blessedness of those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. This supports the prayer’s movement from the present Lord’s Supper to the future feast with Christ.
This passage promises that God’s redeemed people will hunger and thirst no more and will be shepherded by the Lamb. It illuminates the prayer’s hope for final satisfaction in Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The Lord’s Supper is understood differently across Christian traditions, especially regarding Christ’s presence, sacramental efficacy, and who may receive. The adaptation preserves the Puritan/Reformed emphasis on visible signs, faith, spiritual communion with Christ, and assurance through Christ’s death, without defining the issue more narrowly than the original requires.

The original uses the word “emblems,” which can sound merely symbolic in some contemporary contexts. The adaptation keeps the language of bread and cup as signs that truly direct faith to Christ, while also including biblical language of participation from 1 Corinthians 10.
The original’s strong substitutionary and satisfaction language may be doctrinally contested in some circles, but it is central to the prayer and has been preserved rather than softened.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Hide myself beneath his righteousness” was rendered as resting on Christ’s worthiness and taking refuge in his righteousness, to keep the doctrine of justification in natural language.

“Rightly discern and spiritually apprehend the Saviour” was interpreted as asking the Spirit for reverent, faith-filled reception of Christ through the Supper, not mere intellectual understanding or physical reception.

“Opened my side to make you clean” was rendered as being pierced so I could be cleansed, connecting the image to Christ’s crucifixion and the cleansing associated with his blood without over-explaining the Johannine imagery.

“Testify before all men” was adapted as saying with my actions that I gladly receive Jesus, since participation in the Supper is a public confession, though the prayer itself remains personal and singular as requested.
